->FIGARO, *s'avançant.*<-
Moi, qui me rends à vos ordres.

->LE COMTE.<-
Et pourquoi ces mots?

->FIGARO.<-
Je n'ai rien dit.

->LE COMTE, *répétant.*<-
« Ma femme, s'il vous plaît? »

->FIGARO.<-
C'est la fin d'une réponse que je faisais: « Allez le dire à ma femme, s'il vous plaît. »

->LE COMTE, *à part, en se promenant.*<-
Sa femme!... Je voudrais bien savoir quelle affaire peut arrêter monsieur quand je le fais appeler?

->FIGARO, *feignant d'assurer son habillement.*<-
Je m'étais sali sur ces couches en tombant; je me changeais.

->LE COMTE.<-
Faut-il une heure?

->FIGARO.<-
Il faut le temps.

->LE COMTE.<-
Les domestiques ici sont plus longs à s'habiller que les maîtres.

->FIGARO.<-
C'est qu'ils n'ont point de valets pour les y aider.

->LE COMTE.<-
Je n'ai pas trop compris ce qui vous avait forcé tantôt de courir un danger inutile en vous jetant...

->FIGARO.<-
Un danger! on dirait que je me suis engouffré tout vivant...

->LE COMTE.<-
Essayez de me donner le change en feignant de le prendre, insidieux valet! Vous entendez fort bien que ce n'est pas le danger qui m'inquiète, mais le motif.

->FIGARO.<-
Sur un faux avis, vous arrivez furieux, renversant tout, comme le torrent de la Moréna; vous cherchez un homme, il vous le faut, ou vous allez briser les portes, enfoncer les cloisons; je me trouve là par hasard: qui sait, dans votre emportement, si...?

->LE COMTE.<-
Vous pouviez fuir par l'escalier.

->FIGARO.<-
Et vous, me prendre au corridor.

->LE COMTE, *en colère.*<-
Au corridor!... (*A part.*) Je m'emporte, et nuis à ce que je veux savoir.

->FIGARO, *à part.*<-
Voyons-le venir, et jouons serré.

->LE COMTE, *radouci.*<-
Au surplus, ce n'est pas ce que je voulais dire; laissons cela. J'avais, oui, j'avais quelque envie de t'emmener à Londres, courrier de dépêches; mais toutes réflexions faites...

->FIGARO.<-
Monseigneur a changé d'avis?

->LE COMTE.<-
Premièrement, tu ne sais pas l'anglais.

<column-break/>

->FIGARO.<-
Je sais God-dam.

->LE COMTE.<-
Je n'entends pas.

->FIGARO.<-
Je dis que je sais God-dam.

->LE COMTE.<-
Eh bien?

->FIGARO.<-
Diable! c'est une belle langue que l'anglais; il en faut peu pour aller loin. Avec God-dam, en Angleterre, on ne manque de rien nulle part: voulez-vous tâter d'un bon poulet gras? entrez dans une taverne, et faites seulement ce geste au garçon. (*Il fait le geste de tourner la broche.*) God-dam! on vous apporte un pied de bœuf salé sans pain; c'est admirable! Aimez-vous à boire un coup d'excellent Bourgogne, ou de Clairet? rien que celui-ci. (*Il fait le geste de déboucher une bouteille.*) God-dam! on vous sert un pot de bière, en bel étain, la mousse aux bords. Quelle satisfaction! Rencontrez-vous une de ces jolies personnes qui vont trottant menu, les yeux baissés, coudes en arrière, et tortillant un peu des hanches? mettez mignardement tous les doigts unis sur la bouche. Ah! God-dam! elle vous sangle un soufflet de crocheteur; preuve qu'elle entend. Les Anglais, à la vérité, ajoutent par-ci, par-là, quelques autres mots en conversant; mais il est bien aisé de voir que God-dam est le fond de la langue; et si monseigneur n'a pas d'autre motif de me laisser en Espagne...

->LE COMTE, *à part.*<-
Il veut venir à Londres; elle n'a pas parlé.

->FIGARO, *à part.*<-

Figaro?

Quel motif avait la comtesse pour me jouer un pareil tour?

->FIGARO.<-

->LE COMTE.<-
Je la préviens sur tout et la comble de présens.

->FIGARO.<-
Vous lui donnez, mais vous êtes infidèle; sait-on gré du superflu à qui nous prive du nécessaire?

Autrefois tu me disais tout.

->FIGARO.<-
Et maintenant je ne vous cache rien.

->LE COMTE.<-
Combien la comtesse t'a-t-elle donné pour cette belle association?

->FIGARO, *stepping forward.*<-
Here I am, reporting for your orders.

->THE COUNT.<-
And why those words?

->FIGARO.<-
I said nothing.

->THE COUNT, *repeating.*<-
"My wife, if you please?"

->FIGARO.<-
That was the end of a reply I was making: "Go tell it to my wife, if you please."

->THE COUNT, *aside, pacing.*<-
His wife!... I would very much like to know what business can detain this gentleman when I have him summoned?

->FIGARO, *pretending to adjust his clothes.*<-
I got dirty falling into those garden beds; I was changing.

->THE COUNT.<-
Does it take an hour?

->FIGARO.<-
It takes the time it takes.

->THE COUNT.<-
The servants here take longer to dress than their masters.

->FIGARO.<-
That is because they have no valets to help them.

->THE COUNT.<-
I did not quite understand what compelled you earlier to run a pointless risk by throwing yourself...

->FIGARO.<-
A risk! One would think I had swallowed myself up alive...

->THE COUNT.<-
Try to throw me off the scent by pretending to mistake my meaning, insidious valet! You understand perfectly well that it is not the risk that worries me, but the motive.

->FIGARO.<-
On a false report, you arrive furious, overturning everything like the torrent of the Sierra Morena; you are looking for a man, you must have him, or you will smash the doors down and break through the partitions; I happen to be there by chance: who knows, in your fury, if...?

->THE COUNT.<-
You could have fled down the stairs.

->FIGARO.<-
And had you catch me in the hallway.

->THE COUNT, *in anger.*<-
In the hallway!... (*Aside.*) I am losing my temper, and hurting my chances of learning what I want to know.

->FIGARO, *aside.*<-
Let us see what he is getting at, and play our cards close to our chest.

->LE COMTE, *softening.*<-
At any rate, that is not what I meant to say; let us drop the subject. I had, yes, I had some desire to take you along to London as an embassy courier; but on second thought...

->FIGARO.<-
Your Lordship has changed his mind?

->THE COUNT.<-
In the first place, you do not know English.

<column-break/>

->FIGARO.<-
I know "God-dam."

->THE COUNT.<-
I do not follow.

->FIGARO.<-
I say that I know "God-dam."

->THE COUNT.<-
Well, and then?

->FIGARO.<-
Good heavens! English is a fine language; one needs very little of it to go far. With "God-dam" in England, one lacks for nothing anywhere. Do you want to sample a plump fat chicken? Step into a tavern, and merely make this gesture to the waiter. (*He makes the gesture of turning a spit.*) "God-dam!" They bring you a salted ox-foot without bread; it is wonderful! Would you like a drink of excellent Burgundy, or Bordeaux? Nothing more than this. (*He makes the gesture of uncorking a bottle.*) "God-dam!" They serve you a pot of beer in fine pewter, foaming at the brim. What a delight! Do you meet one of those pretty girls who go trotting along with mincing steps, eyes lowered, elbows back, and hips swaying slightly? Daintily bring all your fingertips together to your lips. Ah! "God-dam!" She slaps you across the face like a dockworker; proof that she understands. To be sure, the English add a few other words here and there in conversation; but it is quite plain to see that "God-dam" is the very foundation of the language; and if your Lordship has no other reason for leaving me behind in Spain...

->THE COUNT, *aside.*<-
He wants to come to London; she has not spoken.

->FIGARO, *aside.*<-
He thinks I know nothing; let us work him over a little in his own style.

->THE COUNT.<-
Figaro?

->FIGARO.<-
Excellency?

*THE COUNT draws Figaro close, and familiarly drapes his arm around his neck, leaning on him.*

What motive did the Countess have for playing such a trick on me?

->FIGARO.<-
Faith, your Lordship, you know that better than I.

->THE COUNT.<-
I anticipate her every wish and shower her with presents.

->FIGARO.<-
You give to her, but you are unfaithful; can anyone be grateful for luxuries from one who deprives them of essentials?

->THE COUNT.<-
In the old days, you told me everything.

->FIGARO.<-
And now I hide nothing from you.

# ROWLDRICH.

The following description of Rowldrich is taken from Dr. STUKELEY'S work entitled *A Description of Abury*, Vol. I. pp. 10, *et seq.*

I SHALL begin with *Rowlright*, or rather *Rowldrich*; and, as a specimen of what requisites are sought for in these inquiries, I shall draw them up in a kind of order; which may be useful in all researches of this sort.

1. A situation on high ground, open heaths, by heads of rivers. Rowldrich is a Temple of the Druids of the first kind, a circular work, which has been often taken notice of in print, lying in the north-west part of Oxfordshire, upon high ground, where the counties of Oxford, Warwick, and Gloucester meet. It is near the town of Chipping Norton. Two rivers rise here, that run in quite contrary directions; the *Evenlode*, towards the south part of the kingdom, which, joining the Isis below Woodstock, visits the great luminary of Britain, Oxford, and then meets the *Thames* at Dorchester, the ancient episcopal see of the *Mercian* kingdom. At this Dorchester are fine remains both of Saxon Church antiquity, of Roman, and of British. The inquisitive that prefer our own country antiquities to the vain tour of foreign, will find much of curious amusement there. The other river, Stour, runs from Rowldrich directly north, to meet the Avon at Stratford, thence to the Severn Sea. So that Rowldrich must needs stand on very high ground; and to those who attentively consider the place itself, it appears to be a large cop'd hill, on the summit of an open down; and the Temple, together with the Arch-druid's barrow hard by, stands on the very tip of it, having a descent every way thence; and an extensive prospect, especially into Gloucestershire and Warwickshire. The country hereabouts was originally an open, barren heath; and underneath, a quarry of a kind of ragstone. At present, near here are some inclosures, which have been ploughed up. The major part of our antiquity remains, though many of the stones have been carried away within memory, to make bridges, houses, &c.

2. It is an open temple of a circular form, made of stones set upright in the ground. The stones are rough and unhewn, and were (as I apprehend) taken from the surface of the ground. I saw stones lying in the field near *Norton*, not far off, of good bulk, and the same kind as those of our antiquity. There are such in other places hereabouts, whence the Druids took them; though, in the main, carried off ever since, for building and other uses.

3. We observe the effect of the weather upon these works. This we are treating of stands in the corner of the hedge of the inclosure, near the northern summit of the hill—" a great monument of antiquity," says the excellent Mr. Camden: "a number of vastly great stones placed in a circular figure. They are of unequal height and shape, very much ragged, impaired, and decayed by time." link between the worship of the symbol of personal gener-
ative power and that of the heavenly phallus; as the wor-

A white spider, with very long and very slender legs, ground up in old oil, is also said to remove leukoma by anointing. But even that kind which has the thickest web, usually in rafters, tied up in a cloth, is reported to heal fluxions, as Pliny reports in the same place. Galen, however, omitted medicines made from spiders, as if frivolous and almost superstitious; yet he mentioned their webs to be applied to wounds or ulcers of the outer skin, which remedy is also in very well-known common use whenever someone wounds himself even very slightly with a knife.

The spider's web, however, especially when white and clean, has the power of constricting, and likewise of cooling. Applied to fresh wounds, it preserves them from putrid discharge; it wipes away spots that are still fresh; it heals a recent wound, and prevents inflammation from arising there (as Dioscorides and Pliny write), which does not allow the wound to come to healing. Mixed with certain ointments and applied to the temples, it cures fevers. Dropped into the ear with oil, it calms its pain, on the authority of Avicenna. Wrapped in a cloth and applied to the region of the heart and stomach, it heals tertian agues and trembling of the heart. For a fractured skull, applied with oil and vinegar, it does not come away until the wound is healed; which remedy Serenus also praised:

> *If indeed an injurious blow has crushed the head,*
> *The garment of Arachne must be bound with oil;*
> *It will not know how to leave that place, except when it has healed it.*

The Egyptians prepare a medicament, as Prosper Alpinus <margin>h</margin> reports, from many spiders crushed together with their webs, mixed after the manner of a liniment with rose oil; or they boil down the spiders themselves in the aforesaid oil, with which when warm they anoint the wrists of both hands. Spanish flies <note>original: "Cantharides", blister beetles</note> wrapped in spider webs and hung on a person suffering from quartan fever are reported to free him completely. Aëtius <margin>i</margin> has a wax salve made from spiders, which anyone who wishes may consult. Certain peoples of the Indies devour spiders, especially the people of Chiribichi <note>Chiribichi, an indigenous people of coastal Venezuela</note>, who are otherwise very prone to nausea, so that if they see anything that does not greatly please them, they are moved to nausea and vomiting.

That comparison also seems proverbial: of a spider weaving webs out of itself, and of a man contriving falsehoods out of his own mind. # CONSCIOUSNESS

He who shall be called the Seeker
Ascended into the High Place
Of the Mountain of the Wise.

And in the High Place of the Mount
Sat a most Holy Philosopher
Leaning upon a forked stick.

The Seeker addressed the Ancient Sage,
Imploring wisdom from the Master
Who dwelt alone with the stars.

“Tell me, O Lord of the Seven Peaks,
Of the Mystery of Knowing
And of the Substance of Knowledge.”

Then spoke the Hoary Saint
In slow and solemn voice, his words
Rich with a mystic meaning.

> “The Knower cannot Know.
> There is no Knowing.
> Knowledge is not.”

Bowing his head in helplessness,
The Seeker asked another question:
“Reveal then, O Sage, the inner fact.”

He who leaned upon the forked stick,
Smiled gravely and then replied;
“Ponder well these words, O son of man.”

Nevertheless, that natural conservatism, which is one of the characteristics of the Indian people, was a means of protecting the pictorial art in certain localities, and there are proofs that the traditions of painting were maintained, although somewhat indistinctly, during these long years of religious reconstruction. Transforming influences were at work, but the original handicraft still lived, and was carried on, in spite of the spiritual and political changes to which the whole country was subjected. It is during this rule that indigenous painting, now referred to as Rajput, again comes into view, but the form it took previous to the Mogul dynasty is practically unknown. And he drew him along with him, he could do so at this moment; there was a fire in the young artist's blood, a change in his soul, an urge to tear himself loose from everything old, everything he was accustomed to, tear himself out of his own old self, and today he followed *Angelo*.

On the outskirts of Rome lay an <term>osteria</term> <gloss>tavern</gloss> frequented by artists, built into the ruins of an ancient bath chamber. The large, yellow lemons hung among the dark, glossy foliage and covered part of the old, reddish-yellow walls; the tavern was a deep vault, almost like a cave into the ruin. A lamp burned inside before the image of the Madonna; a great fire blazed on the hearth, where meats were roasted, boiled, and fried; outside, under lemon and laurel trees, stood a couple of laid tables.

Merrily and jubilantly the two were received by their friends; little was eaten, much was drunk, which brought about high spirits; songs were sung and the guitar was played; the <term>saltarello</term> <gloss>a lively Italian jumping dance</gloss> sounded, and the merry dance began. A couple of young Roman girls, models for the young artists, joined in the dance, mingling in the revelry; two lovely bacchantes! Indeed, they did not have the form of Psyche, nor were they delicate, lovely roses, but fresh, vigorous, glowing carnations.

How hot it was on this day, hot even at sunset! Fire in the blood, fire in the air, fire in every glance! The air swam in gold and roses, life was gold and roses.

"‘Trübner's Bibliographical Guide to American Literature’ deserves praise for the great care with which it is prepared, and the wonderful amount of information contained in its pages. It is compiled and edited by Mr. Nicolas Trübner, the publisher, of Paternoster-row. It comprises a classified list of books published in the United States during the last forty years, with Bibliographical Introduction, Notes, and Alphabetical Index. The introduction is very elaborate and full of facts, and must be the work of a gentleman who has spared no pains in making himself master of all that is important in connection with American literature. It certainly supplies much information not generally known in Europe."—*Morning Star*, Jan. 31st, 1859.

“Mr. Trübner deserves much credit for being the first to arrange bibliography according to the received rules of the art. He began the labour in 1855, and the first volume was published in that year; constituting, in fact, the earliest attempt, on this side of the Atlantic, to catalogue American books. The present volume, of course, is enlarged, and is more perfect in every respect. The method of classification is exceedingly clear and useful.

“In short, it presents the actual state of literature, as well as the course of its development from the beginning. Into the subject-matter of this section we shall have to look hereafter, we are now simply explaining the composition of Mr. Trübner's most valuable and useful book.”—*Spectator*, Feb. 5, 1859.

“Mr. Trübner's book is by far the most complete American bibliography that has yet appeared, and displays an amount of patience and research that does him infinite credit. We have tested the accuracy of the work upon several points demanding much care and inquiry, and the result has always been satisfactory. Our American brethren cannot fail to feel complimented by the production of this volume, which in quantity almost equals our own London catalogue.”—*The Bookseller*, Feb. 24th, 1859.

“To say of this volume that it entirely fulfils the promise of its title-page, is possibly the highest and most truthful commendation that can be awarded to it. Mr. Trübner deserves however, something beyond general praise for the patient and intelligent labour with which he has elaborated the earlier forms of the work into that which it now bears. What was once but a scanty volume, has now become magnified, under his care, to one of considerable size; and what was once little better than a dry catalogue, may now take rank as a biographical work of first-rate importance. His position as an American literary agent has, doubtless, been very favourable to Mr. Trübner, by throwing matter in its way; and he confesses, in his preface, that it is to this source that he is mainly indebted for the materials which have enabled him to construct the work before us. Mr. Trübner's object in compiling this book is, he states, two-fold: ‘On the one hand, to suggest the necessity of a more perfect work of its kind by an American, surrounded, as he necessarily would be, with the needful appliances; and, on the other, to supply to Europeans a guide to Anglo-American literature—a branch which, by its rapid rise and increasing importance, begins to force itself more and more on our attention. It is very modest in Mr. Trübner thus to treat his work as a mere suggestion for others. It is much more than this: it is an example which those who attempt to do anything more complete cannot do better than to follow a model, which they will do well to copy, if they would combine fulness of material with that admirable order and arrangement which so facilitates reference, and without which a work of this sort is all but useless.

“All honour, then, to the literature of Young America—for young she still is, and let her thank her stars for it—and all honour also, to Mr. Trübner, for taking so much pains to make us acquainted with it.”—*The Critic*, March 19, 1859.

“This is not only a very useful, because well executed, bibliographical work—it is also a work of much interest to all who are connected with literature. The bulk of it consists of a classified list, with date of publication, size, and price, of all the works, original or translated, which have appeared in the United States during the last forty years; and an alphabetical index facilitates reference to any particular work or author. On the merits of this portion of the work we cannot, of course, be expected to form a judgment. It would require something of the special erudition of Mr. Trübner himself, to say how far he has succeeded or fallen short of his undertaking—how few, or how many, have been his omissions. There is one indication, however, of his careful minuteness, which suggests the amount of labour that must have been bestowed on the work—namely, the full enumeration of all the contents of the various Transaction and Scientific Journals. Thus, ‘the Transactions of the American Philosophical Society,’ from the year 1769 to 1857—no index to which has yet appeared in America—are in this work made easy of reference, every paper of every volume being mentioned seriatim. For in certain connections of bones they are joined to one another in such a way that their composition completely eludes perception, and it seems to be one continuous bone rather than two, just as in the structure of those things that are said to be joined by <term>symphysis</term> <gloss>coalescence</gloss>. In certain others they are joined in a looser manner, and remain two separate bones, touching each other only so that an evident structure easily presents itself to view.

<margin>1. By coalescence.</margin>
Bones are therefore said to be coupled by <term>symphysis</term> <gloss>growing together</gloss> when they are continuous, and so joined together that they coalesce into one and grow together in such a manner that they cannot be separated from one another without breaking one part.

Just as union is twofold: *the first*, which is said to occur of itself, when two divided parts come together with no intervening medium, just as wounds that are said to be cured by first intention; *the other*, which occurs accidentally, through the intervention of something heterogeneous, just as those that are consolidated by second intention, where the lips of the wound are joined together either by flesh

<margin>*Symphysis that lacks a medium.*</margin>
or by scar tissue. In the same way, bones also coalesce with each other, sometimes with no intervening medium, which is true and legitimate union, and sometimes with some intervening medium, which is called less proper <term>symphysis</term> <gloss>growing together</gloss>.

You may observe that former kind in the lower jaw, which from two bones joined by <term>synchondrosis</term> <gloss>cartilaginous union</gloss> turns into a single bone, with that cartilage that intervened between both becoming so ossified that not even a trace of it is left behind afterward. When, therefore, in a human being's first birth,

<margin>Bone.</margin>
the two bones of the jaw were joined by <term>symphysis</term> <gloss>growing together</gloss> improperly so called, they are subsequently coupled by legitimate union once the cartilage has been done away with. Thus, in the bones of a fetus that has emerged from the womb, one will be able to discern innumerable appendages, united by <term>synchondrosis</term> <gloss>cartilaginous union</gloss> and <term>syneurosis</term> <gloss>ligamentous union</gloss>, which later, as the intermediate binding vanishes and passes into a bony nature, are joined to the rest by the primary kind of <term>symphysis</term> <gloss>coalescence</gloss>. Thus also each individual vertebra in infants consists of three small bones joined to each other by cartilage, which shortly afterward turn into one continuous bone. So it is with the innominate bones, and so it is with the sternum.

But here one must carefully note the *cause* that Galen assigned to this diversity of <term>symphysis</term> <gloss>growing together</gloss> in his book *On Bones* <note>original Latin: "libr. de ossibus"</note>. "Soft and spongy bones," he says, "readily coalesce and grow together so as to become one; but those that are hard, solid, and dense require some medium in order to unite. For things that differ greatly from each other in nature, like hard and soft, cannot be united except through a medium. Soft indeed readily grows together with soft; but hard cannot unite with hard unless something intervenes that binds both. Wherefore bones that are drier and denser coalesce through the intervention of another."

Yet since that intermediate medium is threefold, namely cartilage, sinew, and flesh, three species of <term>symphysis</term> <gloss>growing together</gloss> are also commonly posited: <term>synchondrosis</term> <gloss>cartilaginous union</gloss>, <term>syneurosis</term> <gloss>ligamentous union</gloss>, and <term>synsarcōsis</term> <gloss>muscular union</gloss>.
